name: Gripe water

lead: Gripe water is a non-prescription liquid sold in many countries to soothe colic, gas and hiccups in infants. It was created by pharmacist William Woodward in 1851.
It has no direct looks purpose. Parents use it hoping to calm a baby; this entry documents it as a long-running folk remedy and its studies.

paras: Parents give small spoonfuls by mouth. Formulas vary: the original had dill oil, sodium bicarbonate, sugar and alcohol, while modern products use herbs such as fennel, ginger or chamomile.

Health authorities advise against giving it to infants, citing lack of research and variable ingredients. The CDC has warned about lead in some products, and a 2015 Indian study associated its use with more constipation.

chain: Intended to ease gas and colic
angle.text: Gripe water is meant to ease infant colic. It has no direct effect on appearance and is included as a folk-remedy entry.

lead: Gripe water is an over-the-counter herbal liquid given to infants for colic, gas and general fussiness. William Woodward, an English pharmacist, developed it in 1851 and registered the name as a trademark in 1876.[1]

The original formula contained about 3.6% alcohol, dill oil, sodium bicarbonate and sugar. Britain required removal of alcohol in 1992, and in 1993 the US FDA detained Woodward's as an unapproved drug, after which US products were sold as dietary supplements.[1]

A US drug label lists it for irritability, hiccups, gas and colic under homeopathic indications.[2] Systematic reviews of colic treatments are published,[3] but gripe water is not supported by trials, and reviews have advised against its use.[1][4]
infobox: Dill oil, sodium bicarbonate, sugar, alcohol
Sold as dietary supplement or homeopathic product

paras: Woodward drew on treatments for "fen fever" in 1840s eastern England and used the slogan "Granny told Mother and Mother told me."[1] Journal articles tell the product's story and discuss why it is given.[5][6]

A summary of the literature reports health authorities advise against it, noting research is lacking and ingredients vary, and the CDC has warned about lead in some products.[1] A 2012 article asked whether it is baby-friendly.[4]

No studies found specific to gripe water efficacy in randomised trials. Systematic reviews of colic interventions in general exist.[3] A 2015 Indian study of 350 infants reported colic, vomiting and constipation more common in infants given gripe water than in exclusively breastfed infants.[1]
